newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian Socialists promise to restore order.
newsitem.headline: Albanian Socialists promise to restore order.

text.p: Albanian leftist leaders told thousands of supporters in the capital on the last day of a bitterly-fought general election campaign on Friday they were the last hope for restoring order in the troubled Balkan state.

Hundreds of heavily-armed policemen surrounded Tirana's central Skanderbeg Square as Socialist Party chairman Fatos Nano promised a crowd of more than 5,000 he would bring back the smiles back on their faces after months of lawlessness sparked by the crash of a string of shady investment funds.
The square had been off-limits for the Socialists since they were ousted from power by President Sali Berisha's dominant right-leaning Democratic Party in 1992.

"Albania needs peace and calm. It needs the smiles of everybody, especially the children, mothers and sisters. No dictator will take that smile away any more," Nano said. "We will bring you joy, hope and the future."
Berisha was due to speak to his supporters in the same place at around 6 p.m. (1700 GMT) on Friday.

The rallies mark the end of an electoral campaign waged against the backdrop of increasing anarchy and violence, particularly in the south of the povery-stricken nation, which remains largely outside government control.

At least eight people were wounded on Thursday night when shooting erupted during an address by Berisha to supporters in Lushnje, about 80 km (50 miles) south of Tirana. The Democrats later blamed leftist extremists for opening fire on the crowd.

The Democrats have found it practically impossible to campaign in the south, accusing Nano's Socialists, reformed successors of the communists, of using armed gangs to incite violence in a desperate effort to win Sunday's snap polls.

But Nano, 45, blames the unrest on the Democrats' and claims they would strive to reimburse investors for their losses, estimated at some 1.2 billion dollars -- more than half the country's entire output.
The snap election was called to restore some measure of stability in formerly communist Albania after the establishment in March of an interim unity government made up of 10 parties.

The vote is being held 13 months after Albania's third multi-party elections since the collapse of communism in 1990. International observers said the 1996 vote was subject to manipulation and voter intimidation.

The Democrats won 122 of the 140 parliamentary seats then. Berisha, a former heart surgeon, maintained that the vote was held correctly and steadfastly ignored demands from Washington and some European states to rerun it.
But when a number of high-risk pyramid investment schemes collapsed early this year, the government's grip on power began to weaken.

Riding a wave of popularity unseen since four years ago when he was arrested on embezzlement charges -- to be pardoned by Berisha and released in March -- Nano said there was no chance the Socialists would work with Berisha's Democrats should they clinch a majority in Sunday's poll.
"Berisha is not ready to work with anybody in Albania so I very much hope he will have clients as a cardiologist," Nano told reporters as he arrived at the rally.
Sources close to Berisha have told diplomats privately he would step down if the left wins power, but observers believe he will stay on if the vote is close.
